summary: The Birdsmouth cut calculator turns the ridge board thickness, the overhang distance and more into roof pitch angle (θ). It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Birdsmouth cut calculator work?
sections.html:
The Birdsmouth cut calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports roof pitch angle (θ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the ridge board thickness (tridgₑ&ₙbₛₚ;bₒₐrd), the overhang distance (O), the rafter segment run (X) and the rafter segment rise (Y).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Birdsmouth cut calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Roof pitch angle (θ)=(2 × rafter segment rise (Y) ÷ (building width (W) − ridge board thickness (tridgₑ&ₙbₛₚ;bₒₐrd)))
Building width (W)=2 × rafter segment run (X) + ridge board thickness (tridgₑ&ₙbₛₚ;bₒₐrd)
Building width (W)=2 × rafter segment (Lₛₑgₘₑₙₜ) × the cosine of (roof pitch angle (θ)) + ridge board thickness (tridgₑ&ₙbₛₚ;bₒₐrd)
Roof pitch angle (θ)=(heel cut depth (cₕ) ÷ seat cut length (cₛ))
Roof pitch angle (θ)=((1 ÷ 12) × roof pitch (x:12))
Roof pitch angle (θ)=((1 ÷ 4) × minimum rafter depth (dₘiₙ&ₙbₛₚ;rₐfₜₑr) ÷ heel cut depth (cₕ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in meters

  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Birdsmouth cut calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the ridge board thickness, the overhang distance and the rafter segment run — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Birdsmouth cut calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns roof pitch angle (θ), derived from the ridge board thickness, the overhang distance and the rafter segment run. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Birdsmouth cut calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the ridge board thickness, the overhang distance, the rafter segment run and the rafter segment rise, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter building width (W) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Building width (W) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Birdsmouth cut calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
